Title: Contesting at the NAC 2009 and the Week of Nightmares

Messages.Author: The Lasombra
Messages.Body:
I contested three items during the entire Week of Nightmares and the
NAC championship events.

1) The Coven (with both my predator and prey! woo hoo! won that
game)

2) Nosferatu Justicar title (Alonso vs. Sheldon, Sheldon won the
contest, was able to make a shady deal for 2 VPs anyway)

3) Alonso Petrodon (No choice on my part, my prey had 6 on him when I
influenced him into play. My predator was Giovanni power bleed - or
at least seemed to be, so my prey contested him to prevent himself
from bounced bleeds. I made another shady deal for half a VP in that
game. If I had influenced Servius Marius Pustula or Gabrielle di
Righetti first instead it would have been a completely different
game. Antón de Concepción was unable to save me by himself, and a
cross table DI on a Govern, a Pentex on my predator, and an offered
Eagle's Sight block kept me in the game long enough for Antón to make
his appearance.)

What did you contest?
How did that contest affect your games?

On Oct 5, 3:51 pm, The Lasombra <thelasom...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>

In addition to hearing about people's contesting experiences at the
2009 NAC, I'm particularly interested in how it compares to last
year's NAC and the year before. And 5 years before.

I've been observing the various contestation threads for a while now.
And I just managed to figure out how to search the older archives from
the group (hate what Google did to the Search functionality).

The thing that constantly puzzles me is why contestation has suddenly
become such a big issue *now*. With every set, crypt contestation
becomes less and less likely (because more vampires are printed and
new groups are introduced). If the contestation rules were to be
changed, I would have expected a large movement 5 or 10 years ago when
it was a bigger deal. So why *now*?

During the 2009 NAC, there were talks about contesting Sheldon,
Petrodon, and Gabrielle. But at least you had three options for
choosing Nosferatu Justicar (Sheldon, Cock Robin, Petrodon) or Tremere
Justicar (Ulugh Beg, Zagreb, and Gabrielle). Before November 2008, you
only had two options. And before August 2002, you only had one option.
So why is there more complaining and dissatisfaction now, when it
should have been such a larger issue before?

I am especially puzzled about the apparent sea change against the
current contestation rules, especially by people who previously
supported them.

3 years ago, XZealot said:

"With every new edition, contesting gets rarer and rarer. It is less
of a problem than it has ever been. So yes two Gilber Duane decks or
two Tariq decks may show up. That's part of the game, you have to be
able to play around it. Contesting a vampire is certainly a better
option than the no option of getting your vampire nuked with PTOish
cards, Amaranthed, etc... At least, when you contest a vampire you
can
still keep the option of trying to keep the vampire. Unique vampires
are good for the game."

So back then, it was part of the game and something you'd have to play
around. But now Norm has been launching a crusade against the current
rules. What changed?

Similarly, LSJ's previous mode of thought was:

"The point is that building a star vampire deck gets certain benefits
(usually found on the star vampire's card text and Discipline spread),
at the price of certain risks. Players who do not like the way the
probabilities work in such situations (frequent gain balanced out by
infrequent disaster) should be advised to build decks more suited to
their risk tolerance."

and

"Why bother with tinkering with the contesting rules when the tiny
problem it raises (when measured against the ocean you describe) can
already be addressed by the player's own deck building choices? Of
course, if anyone has ideas for rules modifications that would help
reduce the impact of the other things (the stupid, not-your-own-fault
things that can happen in a game to kill your deck), I'd be interested
to read them. But the vagaries of seating order seem sort of inherent
to the game's pred-prey mechanism, which is itself a cornerstone of
the game."

More recently this issue was briefly brought up in a discussion
between Bill Ricardi, LSJ, and wumpus, but I don't think it got as
much attention as it deserved.

James Coupe has been consistently objective over the years, and his
recent comments on Richard Garfield's design notes were particularly
insightful. Even back in 2006, James was advocating the importance of
"Intelligent back-up" so that a star vampire deck could still have
options even if it didn't get its star vampire:

http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/browse_thread/thread/e03a36f377649b7c/bb0c6b26556389f9?q=contesting+group%3Arec.games.trading-cards.jyhad&lnk=ol&

Another interesting older thread is:

http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/browse_thread/thread/a218ef1746e6251c/7b77f4c886de21b2?q=contesting+group:rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad#7b77f4c886de21b2

Where Brian Moritz gets feedback on ways to avoid contesting Gratiano,
the star vampire in his Pander deck. And people provided plenty of
constructive feedback on how to minimize the problem (rather than
railing against the actual contestation rules).

In years past, contestation was regarded as a relatively minor issue.
Why is it suddenly such a big issue now?

Not trying to be snide but the only thing I can think of is that in
years past, people were so used to contesting that it wasn't
considered out of the ordinary. With contestation becoming less and
less likely, people become somewhat "spoiled" but not having to
contest, so that when they actually do they perceive it as a bigger
issue. Kind of like how in pre-industrial societies, death was a
natural part of the lifecycle but in modern societies, death has now
become abnormal rather than normal. I'm guessing this is what Peter
Bakija was alluding to in his comment about how contesting used to be
"less of a random misery phase and more of a reliable function of the
game." But I still find it ironic that contesting has apparently
become a bigger issue precisely because it has become less and less
likely.

Messages.Author: D.J.
Messages.Body:
On Oct 6, 1:40 pm, echiang...@yahoo.com wrote:
> In years past, contestation was regarded as a relatively minor issue.
> Why is it suddenly such a big issue now?

Well, in most of those threads, the issue hasn't been about actually
contesting, and it's certainly not been about star vampires. It's
about the random screw-over that happens when, with no cause to be
suspicious that it might, the vampire you just happen to be *about* to
bring out, pops out somewhere else on the table. That's only, really,
a problem when it's a big vampire, but it leaves you with two choices,
most of the time:
1) roll over, start transferring to someone else, and watch your now-
two-turns-and-8-pool-behind game evaporate into a big pile of "you
lose", or
2) bring the vamp out anyway, contest, and drag the other guy down
with you, since you're both out 9+ pool and 3+ turns.

A star vampire deck really only has the second option, and is still
screwed under any of the proposed changes to how contesting unique
crypt cards might work - and that's all well and good, because, as
stated, that's part of what a star vampire deck is.

Why now? Here's my theory:
A lot of work has gone in, in recent years, to making bigger vampires
more playable, more usable. The contestation-lottery-hosing has thus
become more pronounced and more evident, and it's also much, much more
bolt-out-of-the-blue random. Midcaps and weenies aren't hit by it,
really. So it's not really doing anything other than hosing over big-
cap vampires, which is exactly what the design team seems to be trying
to reverse the trend toward.

- D.J.

Here's a question for Jeff and Norm:

Did you ever consider announcing your plans to transfer out Petrodon/
Sheldon before actually putting him directly into play?

It seems like many people treat crypt contestation like a game of
chicken - who's willing to contest and who's willing to back down.
Oftentimes, the onus appears to fall on the second player who
"chooses" to contest. (For those familiar with law, it's somewhat
reminiscent of the Last Clear Chance Doctrine often used in tort
liability for train/car/horse accidents).

Have people thought about making clear their intentions at an earlier
point? Thinking about years and years worth of games, I can only
recall a few occasions where people have actually bothered to do so
when in fact it would be beneficial to do so far more often.

In Jeff's case, the choice of Petrodon is arbitrary (i.e. any of his
vampires can do). So before deciding which vampire to place his first
transfers on, he can announce "I'm going to be transferring to a
vampire with inferior Fortitude, inferior Thaumaturgy, and +1 bleed.
Anyone have problems with that?" AFAIK, Petrodon is the only vampire
who meets those three criteria. (And you don't necessary have to state
which of those disciplines you're actually using).

In Norm's case, once Sheldon had 5 counters and he's about to put the
final 4 on, he could have asked "I'm about to bring out Sheldon unless
someone has any objections." In this case there would still be a
conflict, but they could have avoided a lot of the heartache by
dealing with the problem before it actually came up. Even if Norm was
willing to then transfer to a different vampire, this would have saved
him an additional turn of transfers.

So instead of getting frustrated at the second person who brings a
unique vampire into play, why isn't the first person doing more to
avoid such a situation? If anything, I think it would be especially
prudent to do so when you're about to bring out any 9+ vampire into
play.

Thoughts?

But the thing is, much of this is quite avoidable if people actually
bothered to communicate.

What most people do: My turn, I put four transfers and bring out
Violette Prentiss. Afterwards either A.) Oops! I didn't realize that
my cross-table ally built his deck around Violette and now it's too
late to do anything about it, or B.) Oops! I wasn't paying attention
and didn't realize that Violette Prentiss is already in play, leading
to an accidental contest.

What you could do: My turn. Tell people, "I'm about to put four
transfers on Violette Prentiss and bring her out." People can remind
you that she's already in play or that they really need her instead.
Then you can proceed to bring her out or bring a different vampire
(i.e. Mariana Gilbert) out instead.

What most people do: Recklessly bring out a large capacity vampire
without looking around or talking to other players. Leads to problems
when someone else is also trying to get that same vampire, but the
problem only becomes an issue once the vampire actually hits play.

Option 1: Alluded to in the Sheldon case. Simply announce who you're
going to bring out right before making the final four transfers. Quite
a minimal change. You don't give away any sensitive info (you're about
to bring him into play anyway). And if there is a problem, you can
talk about it before making an irrevocable decision (and saving you 4
transfers if you do change your mind).

Option 2: Alluded to in the Petrodon case. You do reveal a bit more
information about which vampire you're trying to get, but then you
largely avoid the contestation problem (except in cases where someone
strategically wants to contest with you, which is rather cornercase).

I don't want to get all philosophical, but this definitely has some

should we completely change the traffic and road system because some
idiots are still going to try and run a red light.

I guess my main concern is that the contestation rule is just a
symptom of the problem, not the root cause. Yes, it can exacerbate the
situation when things go wrong, but there are better solutions that
can prevent things from going wrong in the first place (i.e.
communication).

For example, some of the other examples have involved accidental
contestation. People simply aren't paying attention (i.e. not looking
across the table to see that vampire is already in play). The problem
isn't with the rules as much as player behavior. And what can you do?
Force people to be more attentive?

In the case that you described, if people simply aren't playing by the
rules (i.e. not making proper announcements) that's a completely
different problem with a different root cause.

Similar issues exist with library cards and talking about things
beforehand can be quite beneficial. But at least people do tend to
talk about library cards more often (though it's still far from
perfect). The classic example is DI. Many times, it's kind of like
"Well you should have talked about what you were going to play instead
of immediately playing it and forcing me to DI your card."

I guess I'd say that if you're really having personal problems with
contestation (and it's really ruined your game), you should at least
first try changing your own behavior before expecting the entire
system and rules to change for you. Even though announcing what
vampire you're bringing out is not required, the benefits may very
well outweigh the negatives. And it's such an easy change that I'm
surprised people don't at least give it a try before advocating a
large, systemic disruption in the established rules.

> And it still won't help you if someone else decides to encourage your investment
> only to then bring out the vampire anyhow (expecting that, since you asked,
> you're adverse to actually making the contest happen).

That's a fair point. But then that person loses their credibility. And
if he ends up having later problems with contestation, that's his
problem. And as previously mentioned and referenced, most of the time
both players lose out by contesting minions.

Sidebar: All this talk about contestation has made me nostalgic about
old school Betrayer decks. Now those were the days... ;-)

I'm interested in a case study with the proposed solution. I was just
talking to Bob on #vtes, so I hope I have the details right. Someone
please correct me if I don't.

Norm->Michael->Bob->Ferenc

Norm goes first and gets Sheldon on turn 3. Bob has 7 on Sheldon. What
happened is Sheldon got Pentexed and could do nothing and Bob had to spend
two more turns getting Selma out. Basically these guys couldn't do
anything because they were crippled in the early game and lost. They lost
the "contestation lottery."

So if I'm not mistaken, the proposed change is that when contesting, one
can choose to pay a pool during untap as normal or one can remove the
(crypt) card from the game to gain the pool back from that card.

Would this help Norm and Bob? Bob could contest Sheldon on turn 3, which
would make Norm pay an extra pool and miss a turn (which was missed anyway
due to Pentex), then Bob could get his 9 pool back on his turn, but now
he's not getting Selma until turn 6. Ouch. I'd say the game is still
lost. It's not going to make much difference.

Or Bob could get Selma on turn 5, contest Sheldon later to get the pool
back, but he's still behind due to not having gotten his important vampire
on turn 3. Getting into the game on turn 5-6 is pretty much a death
sentence.

For my money, the problem isn't contestation and the fact that you might
wind up in a situation like what Bob and Norm had. The problem is that
high cap vampires are inherently weak in vtes. You invest around 1/3 of
your pool in a vampire that could become contested, get Pentexed right
away (and you won't have another vampire to try to remove it for a couple
turns) or you could get Disarmed by Koko and diablerized by Smudge right
away. If Norm and Bob had contested Duck, they would've been fine.

Or look at it like this: Norm gets Sheldon out. Somebody Pentexes him
before he gets an action off. Nobody contests Sheldon. Nobody can/will
remove the Pentex right away. Norm is still probably just as hosed as he
would be in any of the above scenarios.

I guess it wouldn't be hard to come up with scenarios where the rule
change does save somebody's game, but I really think in general that if
you spend 3 turns putting pool on a vampire and then wind up not being
able to get that vampire, you're going to lose, even if you can get the
pool back.

Matt Morgan

> it was a bigger deal. So why *now*?

Jeff raised the issue since the NAC is one of the handful of high
profile VTES tournaments which occur each year, so it is a great test
case. Unlike many local events where people often try to prove points
by winning with conventionally weaker clans or forcing a specific
strategy, people play with good cards at the continental
championships. The likelihood of contestation at such an event is
higher than you would otherwise expect at a garden variety tournament.
Three Parity Shift decks made the finals. That single card really
focuses the attention on some 80-ish vampires who have Prince or
Justicar titles. Cut out about half of those again because they lack
DOM/FOR/OBF/PRE or are just plain bad and you've got a pretty tight
group from which to select.

> In years past, contestation was regarded as a relatively minor issue.
> Why is it suddenly such a big issue now?
>
> Not trying to be snide but the only thing I can think of is that in
> years past, people were so used to contesting that it wasn't
> considered out of the ordinary. With contestation becoming less and
> less likely, people become somewhat "spoiled" but not having to
> contest, so that when they actually do they perceive it as a bigger
> issue. Kind of like how in pre-industrial societies, death was a
> natural part of the lifecycle but in modern societies, death has now
> become abnormal rather than normal. I'm guessing this is what Peter
> Bakija was alluding to in his comment about how contesting used to be
> "less of a random misery phase and more of a reliable function of the
> game." But I still find it ironic that contesting has apparently
> become a bigger issue precisely because it has become less and less
> likely.

I also think that since LSJ and the design team have been working hard
to make large-cap vampires more playable, amazingly, people are
playing them more often! And the new ones are generally better than
the old ones so that focuses the field yet again.

Contestation may just be flavor of the month, but there are always
those who are going to come up with ideas on how to improve the game
we all love so dearly. But I think it really is one of the more
important problems remaining in VTES. PTO, seat-changers, and Edge
Explosion were banned. Weenies got hosed with Scourge of the
Enochians. It's just the next thing that might need fixing and it's
good to debate even if nothing ever comes of it.

Jeff

Well, it's all about trade-offs.

I mean if you think about it, each time you discard (especially near
the beginning of the game), you are revealing information about your
deck to the other players. But in those cases, the perceived benefit
(cycling through your deck to get the card you need) outweighs the
perceived cost (revealing information).

The same applies here. In some cases, the perceived benefit (avoiding
contestation) may exceed the perceived cost (people have a better idea
of what you're playing).

In addition, there are plenty of ways to communicate information
without tipping your hand. Obviously spilling the beans with "I'm
bringing out Petrodon" is probably a bit bone-headed. But there are
ways to describe a vampire without revealing too much. As previously
suggested, you could say that he has inferior Fortitude, inferior
Thaumaturgy, and +1 bleed. Most people won't instantly think "oh it
must be Petrodon." They might think "okay probably not a weenie. Could
be a fattie. Or maybe one of those weird Jyhad/DS/AH era mid-caps with
weird disciplines." Furthermore, if you're clever you can confuse your
opponents by having them draw the wrong assumptions (without even
needing to lie). In this case, people might think you're playing a
bleedy Tremere deck, or a Weather Control / Dawn Op deck (when the
standard Nos deck doesn't even use Fortitude or Thaumaturgy).

So when done poorly, obviously you're giving up a competitive
advantage. But there are plenty of ways to carefully disclose such
information in a way consistent with *excellent* game play.

Then again, maybe that's asking for too much from some players? :-)

I concur with Matt's assessment. Contestation is one of the more
visible examples/symptoms, but it's not the core problem.

Putting all your eggs in one basket is inherently a risky strategy,
and that's especially the case with high pool investments (large
capacity vampires, expensive locations/allies which are just as easily
burned as free ones, etc.). LSJ and the White Wolf design team have
made significant strides over the years to make large caps more
competitive (individual vampires are significantly stronger than in
years past, new cards that make large vampires more attractive, cards

that the issue has not been fully resolved.

you still have the same underlying problem.

disabled (contested, Pentexed, Sensory Deprived, immediately torpored
or burned) you're probably going to have lots of trouble because
you've wasted a lot of time and resources on a single card. Does
situations are going to be just as disruptive as if you had contested
him.

because he had 7 pool on his own Sheldon, the same scenario could
easily happen through non-contestation examples. A well-timed Kaymakli
Nightmares can easily set you two turns back - what if that was the

earlier? Or Brainwash, Cairo International Airport, Lazar Dobrescu,
Trick of the Danya, Banishment, Gemini, or Solomon Batanea could just
as easily set you back 1 or more turns. If your predator uses Solomon
Batanea and Information Highway each turn to nullify 3 of your
transfers, you're going to be having trouble regardless of
contestation. (Hypothetically, he could bring out Info Highway +
Solomon on his first turn, play Kaymakli Nightmares and influence out
Gemini during his second turn. Which means you will probably not be
able to bring out a vampire larger than 4-capacity for most of the
game. A bit contrived yeah but it's just to illustrate the underlying
point).

saying "I'm about to transfer out a minion whose name rhymes with
"Bleldon, Blord of the Blog"--anyone else?"

Being in a situation where someone wants the same big minion as you,
regardless of communication, is both incredibly random and incredibly
debilitating. And occasionally just ends your (where "your" = "both
players involved") game right there. It might take a few turns to
stick, but if two players both want the same big minion, one of them,
if not both of them, are probably completely screwed. Due to pure,
random, dumb luck.

> What most people do: Recklessly bring out a large capacity vampire

How is it "reckless" to start transferring out a big minion when your
deck uses big minions, and then randomly see the same minion hit the
other side of the table?

As someone who was in the thick of this discussion last time, no one
is suggesting removing contestation. Just lessening the incredibly
harsh penalty that comes from getting struck by lightning. Again, a
nice, simple solution is:

"During your untap phase, if you have a contested minion, you may pay
a pool to continue contesting the minion *or* burn the minion and move
all the blood on that minion to your pool."

This might not be the absolute best solution, but it solves a
significant amount of the incredibly harsh and random punishment of
contestation. And has the handy side effect of a lessening benefit if
you already used that minion significantly (i.e. if someone contests
your Arika, and you burn her instead of contesting her, but she only
has 1 blood on her, you only get 1 blood back. But presumably, you did
something good with the other 10 already).

Jeff's original intent was apparently solely to gather information.
But others could easily view the thread as an opportunity to complain

situation, someone could easily use exactly such a thread to
politicize their pro- or anti-contestation views. (If you didn't see

think that was the underlying motive in this case, but an outwardly
neutral query can easily be used as a cover to further another
objective (see classical books about Lying with Statistics).

context (comparing it to previous years, which was my first comment,
though things admittedly digressed after that). For example, this is
underscored by brandonsantacruz comment, "That sucks to have so much
contestation." Was there really that much contestation or did it just
appear so? If there was twice as much contestation in NAC 2008, and
five times as much contestation in NAC 2004, then actually
brandonsantacruz drew the incorrect conclusion because there really
wasn't that much contestation. This is further complicated since
psychology and sociology elements also heavily influence one's
"perception" over recent vs past events.

importance of temporal context, so that people could better evaluate
the 2009 experience instead of looking at it in potentially biased
isolation. Sorry once again that the topic did eventually stray.

Pentex on Isabel de Leon, I'm probably fine. If I play Cesewayo wall and

table dynamics as often such decks will take one VP and then die, but it
sucks to be that one VP and be unable to play because you chose to go
with an Eze deck instead of 1 cap hack.

help both cases. You couldn't have unintentional contestation (unless
players are stupid) because vampires would come into play in a single
turn. This preserves intentional contestation, which I like. It also
could remove the inherent slowness of large vampires, which is part of the
problem.

I think there have been a number of decent undue influence variations
suggested. Maybe something like go with normal influence rules if you're
transferring to/from multiple vampires or you can use all your transfers
to fill a vampire from your pool. That would be pretty simple. This
would be the death of weenie title-grabber vote. Is that a bad thing?

KUTA TRANSFER RULES are just like the normal transfer rules, except:
1) Players get 5 transfers instead of 4.
2) It costs 1 transfer to move a minion (that has counters equal to or
greater than its capacity) from the uncontrolled region to the ready
region.
3) It costs 5 transfers plus 1 pool to move a minion from the top of
the crypt to the uncontrolled region.

Notes:
- On the first turn of the game, Player 1 gets only 1 transfer, Player
2 gets 2, etc., up to 5 transfers for Player 5.

- Rule #2 only applies to bringing minions to the ready region in the
"normal" way. Cards like Tomb of Rameses III, Gather, Chain of
Command, and Web of Knives Recruit don't cost extra transfers.

Slows down weenies. Speeds up fatties. Everyone wins.

Some of the proposed contestation avoidance rules (e.g. remove a
contested vampire from the game and move all blood to your pool) don't
solve the problem of large caps being inherently weaker, but it does
mitigate the risk of playing large cap vampires, which is still not
such a horrible thing.

Jeff
